title: The Closure of a (Pre)connected Set Is (Pre)connected
description: Formalizes the topological fact that the closure of a preconnected set is preconnected (and likewise for connected sets), with its sharper 'bark and tree' generalization — any set wedged between a preconnected set and its closure is preconnected — and the corollary that a dense connected subset makes the whole space connected. Built on Mathlib's IsPreconnected.closure / IsConnected.closure / IsPreconnected.subset_closure, with the dense corollary proved here. 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext:
Connectedness is one of the basic topological invariants: a set is preconnected if it cannot be split by two disjoint open sets each meeting it, and connected if it is additionally nonempty. A fundamental stability property is that connectedness survives taking closures — adding limit points to a connected set keeps it connected. The reason is that any open separation of the closure restricts to an open separation of the original (dense) set, which is impossible. In fact a sharper statement holds, sometimes called the 'bark and tree' theorem: any set wedged between a preconnected set s and its closure is itself preconnected.

These facts are foundational and present in Mathlib (IsPreconnected.closure, IsConnected.closure, IsPreconnected.subset_closure). This entry packages them in gallery form and derives a useful corollary: if a space contains a dense connected subset, the whole space is connected — a common way to prove connectedness (e.g. a space is connected if a dense subspace such as the rationals' image, or a path-connected dense part, is connected).
overview.problemStatement: Prove that the closure of a preconnected set is preconnected, and of a connected set is connected; that any set between a preconnected set and its closure is preconnected ('bark and tree'); and that a dense connected (resp. preconnected) subset makes the whole space connected (resp. preconnected).
overview.proofStrategy: The closure results and 'bark and tree' are invoked from Mathlib (IsPreconnected.closure, IsConnected.closure, IsPreconnected.subset_closure). For the dense corollary, a space is connected iff its universal set is connected (connectedSpace_iff_univ); a dense set has closure equal to the universe (Dense.closure_eq), so univ = closure s, and the closure of a connected set is connected (IsConnected.closure) — giving IsConnected univ and hence ConnectedSpace.
keyInsights: Connectedness cannot be destroyed by adding limit points: an open separation of the closure would already separate the dense original set.
The sharp form is 'bark and tree': any set t with s ⊆ t ⊆ closure s inherits preconnectedness — closing all the way is just the special case t = closure s.
A dense connected subset upgrades to a connected whole space, because its closure is everything and the closure of a connected set is connected.
Reducing global connectedness (ConnectedSpace) to connectedness of a dense part is a standard and reusable technique, e.g. for proving spaces built from connected dense skeletons are connected.
Working at the level of IsPreconnected / IsConnected on Set α (not just on the whole space) keeps the statements maximally reusable for subsets.

The preconnected and connected forms of the density corollary are not interchangeable: ConnectedSpace requires nonemptiness while PreconnectedSpace does not, so the preconnected version holds even for the empty space and needs no nonemptiness witness — a distinction worth keeping explicit for downstream reuse.

sections.title: Overview: Connectedness Is Stable Under Closure
sections.summary: Imports and module docstring. States the topological fact that the closure of a (pre)connected set is (pre)connected, its sharper 'bark and tree' generalization (any set wedged between s and closure s is preconnected), and the corollary that a dense connected subset forces the whole space to be connected. Notes the core results live in Mathlib (IsPreconnected.closure, IsConnected.closure, IsPreconnected.subset_closure) and are packaged here in gallery form with the density corollary added. sections.mathContext: $s$ preconnected $\Rightarrow \overline{s}$ preconnected; more sharply $s \subseteq t \subseteq \overline{s} \Rightarrow t$ preconnected; and a dense connected subset $\Rightarrow$ the space is connected.

conclusion.summary: A fully verified (0 sorries, 0 axioms, no native_decide) file of 75 lines and 6 theorems on the stability of connectedness under closure: the closure of a (pre)connected set is (pre)connected, the 'bark and tree' generalization (any set between s and closure s is (pre)connected), and the corollary that a dense connected subset makes the whole space connected.
conclusion.implications: These package fundamental topological facts in gallery form and add the reusable corollary connecting density to global connectedness. The dense-subset technique is a common route to proving a space is connected; the 'bark and tree' theorem is the sharp tool behind it. All results are stated on subsets (IsPreconnected / IsConnected on Set α) for maximal reusability.
openQuestions: Formalize the analogous stability for path-connectedness or local connectedness, where closure behaves differently (path-connectedness is NOT closure-stable in general).
Use the dense-connected corollary to prove connectedness of specific spaces built from dense connected skeletons.

crossReferences.description: Sibling that probes the limits of this entry's closure-stability: path-connectedness is NOT closure-stable in general (the 'connected salvage' and path-component rigidity), exactly the open question flagged here.

The topologist's sine curve is the canonical example where this entry's theorem bites: a connected set whose closure is connected but not path-connected — concretely realizing 'closure preserves connectedness'.
